entry.title: SAP UI Integration Cards: Choosing the Right Development Path for Supplier Portals
entry.content:
Supplier Portal projects keep finding their way onto my calendar. Across industries, such as manufacturing, retail, energy, public sector, the pattern repeats: a company runs SAP in the back office, has hundreds or thousands of external suppliers, and needs to give those suppliers a meaningful digital touchpoint without onboarding them into the core system. SAP BTP, and specifically SAP Build Work Zone, is increasingly the answer. If I had to pick a top-5 use case for BTP, this is on the list and the reason is almost always the same: you need to give people outside your company controlled, identity-aware access to your processes. That is a non-trivial problem, and BTP is well-positioned to solve it cleanly.

What I also enjoy about this topic is how many technology layers it touches at once. Identity and access management, OData APIs, low-code tooling, process automation, UI frameworks, a Supplier Portal brings them all into play. It is one of those projects where a good architect genuinely has to think across the stack.

I am also speaking at the SAP Exploration Workshop: Supplier Portal later this year, so this has been on my mind a lot recently. This post grew out of preparation for that event,  specifically the question of how to explain UI Integration Cards to developers and architects who are new to the topic but need to make real implementation decisions fast.

The question teams consistently hit early is not what cards are, but which development path to take and when. There are two fundamentally different approaches:

  • Low-code (declarative): Everything lives in manifest.json. No JavaScript controller, no XML view, no build step. The framework handles rendering, theming, accessibility, and responsiveness. This covers eight of the nine card types and the vast majority of supplier portal use cases.
  • Pro-code (Component card): A full SAPUI5 component embedded in a card frame. Maximum flexibility, but you give up automatic theming, the Admin Console configuration panel, and declarative data binding and you take on full responsibility for Fiori compliance and the code maintenance.

Choosing the wrong path creates rework. This post maps both paths with supplier portal context throughout, then gives you a decision framework and highlights the manifest.json patterns, especially Work Zone context bindings and conditional expressions, that are rarely documented in one place.

All code examples are grounded in the official SAP UI5 Card Explorer.

The manifest.json Skeleton — Quick Anatomy

Every card, regardless of type or complexity, uses the same three-namespace structure: sap.app (card identity and metadata), sap.ui (UI5 technology declaration), and sap.card (type and content). The non-negotiable rules: sap.app/type must be "card" (not "application"), sap.app/id must be globally unique across your BTP tenant (use reverse-domain notation), and sap.card/type is the only always-required property within sap.card. For the full schema reference, see the Card Manifest Reference.

{
  "_version": "1.15.0",
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.supplier.cards.my-card",
    "type": "card",
    "applicationVersion": { "version": "1.0.0" }
  },
  "sap.ui": { "technology": "UI5" },
  "sap.card": { "type": "List" }
}

Everything else, such as header, data source, content layout, parameters, destinations is added inside sap.card.

Card Types at a Glance

Eight types are declarative (low-code). One (Component) is the pro-code escape hatch. For the full type documentation and live examples, browse the SAP UI5 Card Explorer directly.

Type Available In Best For

ListSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Orders, alerts, notifications, item feeds
TableSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Inventory tables, reports, structured comparisons
ObjectSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Supplier profiles, order details, record mastercards
TimelineSAPUI5 onlyOnboarding milestones, approval histories, activity logs
AnalyticalSAPUI5 onlyKPI tiles, spend dashboards, bar/donut/line charts
CalendarSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Appointment scheduling, event streams
AdaptiveCardSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Microsoft Adaptive Cards spec content
WebPageSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Embedded web page / iFrame
ComponentSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Full SAPUI5 component — pro-code only

Supplier Portal Use Cases - Card Type Mapping

Before choosing a card type, map your use case to the right type. The table below covers the most common supplier portal scenarios:

Supplier Portal Use Case Card Type Typical Data Source Key manifest.json Pattern

Open purchase orders feedListConditional highlight expression on order amount
Delivery alerts & quality notificationsListhighlight: Error/Warning/Success driven by status field
Invoice status overviewTableOne column per field; "identifier": true on invoice ID
Supplier master data / company profileObjectWork Zone context binding for auto-personalization
Spend KPIs & budget consumptionAnalyticalNumeric header + StackedColumn chart
Delivery performance trendAnalyticalLine or bar chart with trend indicator in header
Onboarding milestone trackerTimelinePer-item icon expression on task status field
Approval history logTimelineChronological task events with dateTime binding
Upcoming supplier calls & meetingsCalendarAppointment template with start/end ISO binding
Custom multi-tab scorecard or map viewComponentFull SAPUI5 component — pro-code path required

Path 1 — Low-Code: Manifest-Only Development

The low-code path covers all eight declarative types. You configure everything, such as data source, layout, interactions inside manifest.json. The framework handles rendering, theming, accessibility, and responsiveness.

For full manifest examples and interactive live previews of each type, the SAP UI5 Card Explorer is the authoritative reference. The four supplier portal scenarios below call out the manifest.json patterns worth understanding before you start: things the documentation covers individually but rarely connects together.

List Card - Open Orders & Alerts

→ Card Explorer: List Card

The List Card is the workhorse for feed-style data: open purchase orders, delivery alerts, quality notifications. Two patterns to know:

  • Binding expressions on highlight, icon, and info fields drive conditional UX entirely declaratively, no controller needed. Syntax: {= ${Amount} > 100000 ? 'Warning' : 'Success'}. The {= ... } expression form works anywhere a string value is expected in the manifest.
  • Configurable parameters ({{parameters.maxItems}}) let portal admins adjust list length in the Admin Console without touching the manifest, making the same card reusable across multiple portal pages with different display needs. Always add withCredentials: true to data.request so the app router forwards the user's Work Zone session to the backend.

Object Card - Supplier Profile

→ Card Explorer: Object Card · Object Card in Focus - SAP Community, Jul 2026

The Object Card renders a single business record as grouped label/value pairs. It is the natural fit for a supplier's master data view. The key pattern: wire a parameter like supplierId to {context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value} (see the Work Zone Context Bindings section below) so the card auto-loads the current user's profile on every page load without any server-side identity resolution logic.

Analytical Card - KPI Dashboard & Spend Charts

→ Card Explorer: Analytical Card

The Analytical Card pairs a "type": "Numeric" header, such as KPI figure, unit, trend indicator, and up to two side indicators with a chart body (StackedColumn, bar, Donut, Line). Use it for spend dashboards, delivery performance KPIs, or quality rate trends on the supplier homepage. Start with inline data.json for a static prototype, then swap in a data.request block to pull from a live OData or REST endpoint. Requires full SAPUI5.

Timeline Card - Onboarding Progress

→ Card Explorer: Timeline Card

The Timeline Card renders ordered, time-stamped events. It is the right choice for supplier onboarding milestone trackers or approval histories. Combine with a {{parameters.currentUser}} context binding (see below) to scope the timeline to the logged-in supplier's workflow instances. Binding expressions work on icon.src too: {= ${status} === 'COMPLETED' ? 'sap-icon://accept' : 'sap-icon://pending'} drives per-item icons dynamically with no controller.

Connecting Cards to SAP BTP Destinations

When a card runs inside SAP Build Work Zone, all backend calls are proxied through the application router. You cannot use absolute backend URLs, but you must declare named destinations and reference them as {{destinations.myDestination}}.

The BTP destination (BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations) must include these additional properties:

Property Required Value Why

HTML5.DynamicDestinationtrueMandatory. Allows the app router to resolve the destination dynamically at runtime. Without it, card requests return 404 or fail silently.
WebIDEEnabledtrueRequired for SAP Business Application Studio tooling to detect the destination.
WebIDEUsageodata_genUse odata_abap for ABAP systems; SuccessFactorsExtensionCard for SuccessFactors.

Declare the destination in the manifest under configuration.destinations:

{
  "sap.card": {
    "configuration": {
      "destinations": {
        "s4hana": {
          "name": "MY_S4H_DESTINATION",
          "defaultUrl": "/sap/opu/odata/sap/",
          "label": "S/4HANA Backend"
        }
      }
    },
    "data": {
      "request": {
        "url": "{{destinations.s4hana}}/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner",
        "parameters": { "$format": "json", "$top": "10" },
        "withCredentials": true
      },
      "path": "/d/results"
    }
  }
}

The name property maps the manifest's logical alias (s4hana) to the physical BTP destination name. This indirection means you can change the target system without editing the manifest. This is very useful when promoting cards across landscapes.

Work Zone Context Bindings 

This is one of the most practically useful patterns in the card framework, and one of the least documented in one place. Work Zone injects a set of context variables at runtime that you can bind directly to card parameters to enable personalized, identity-aware cards with zero server-side user resolution logic.

Here is an example using the Context Bindings as a data. 

"configuration": {
  "parameters": {
    "currentUserId": {
      "value": "{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    },
    "tenantHost": {
      "value": "{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/webHost/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    },
    "sfUserId": {
      "value": "{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/id/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    }
  }
}

Once declared, reference them anywhere in the manifest with {{parameters.currentUserId}} — including inside data.request.url, $filter query parameters, or request headers.

Complete Context Variable Reference

Context Variable Description Availability

{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}Logged-in user's UUID in Work ZoneWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/name/value}Logged-in user's display nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/email/value}Logged-in user's email addressWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/firstName/value}User's first nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/lastName/value}User's last nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/id/value}Work Zone company/tenant IDWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/webHost/value}Tenant web host (for constructing URLs)WZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/id/value}SAP SuccessFactors user IDSuccessFactors Work Zone
{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/name/value}SAP SuccessFactors display nameSuccessFactors Work Zone

Practical use cases for supplier portals:

  • Personalized data fetch: use currentUser/id to filter an OData query to the current supplier's records.
  • Dynamic URL construction: use currentCompany/webHost to build tenant-specific deep links in navigation actions.
  • SuccessFactors cross-scenario: if your supplier portal also hosts HR self-service cards, sap.successfactors/currentUser/id lets you target SF OData endpoints without a separate identity resolution call.

Path 2 — Pro-Code: Component Cards

The Component card type loads a full SAPUI5 component. Essentially it is a mini-application embedded in a card frame. Choose this path only when:

  • Your layout cannot be expressed by any of the eight declarative types (e.g., a custom multi-tab view, a map widget, a D3 chart).
  • You need complex client-side business logic (multi-step form validation, dynamic data dependencies between fields).
  • You are wrapping an existing SAPUI5 application fragment as a card.

The manifest for a Component card delegates rendering to SAPUI5:

{
  "_version": "1.15.0",
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.supplier.cards.custom-scorecard",
    "type": "card",
    "applicationVersion": { "version": "1.0.0" }
  },
  "sap.card": {
    "type": "Component",
    "header": {
      "title": "Supplier Scorecard",
      "subTitle": "Custom performance view"
    }
  },
  "sap.ui5": {
    "rootView": {
      "viewName": "com.company.supplier.cards.custom-scorecard.view.Main",
      "type": "XML",
      "async": true
    },
    "dependencies": {
      "minUI5Version": "1.90.0",
      "libs": {
        "sap.ui.core":   {},
        "sap.m":         {},
        "sap.ui.layout": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

The corresponding project structure adds a full SAPUI5 component alongside the manifest:

my-component-card/
├── manifest.json
├── Component.js            ← SAPUI5 UIComponent
├── view/
│   └── Main.view.xml       ← XML view
├── controller/
│   └── Main.controller.js
└── i18n/
    └── i18n.properties

The architectural cost to factor in: Component cards require you to manually implement SAP Fiori design guidelines. The automatic theming, accessibility guarantees, and Admin Console configuration panel that declarative cards provide for free become your responsibility. This also means that when SAP updates Work Zone's design system or theming tokens, your Component card will not automatically pick up the changes. 

Decision Framework: Which Path Should You Choose?

Use these questions to reach the right decision before writing any code:

Question If YES → Recommendation

Does your data fit a list, table, object, chart, or timeline pattern?Low-CodeUse the corresponding declarative type
Do you need the card to be configurable by portal admins (no code)?Low-CodeUse configuration.parameters
Is the card connecting to a single BTP destination OData/REST endpoint?Low-CodeDeclarative data.request handles this
Do you need per-user personalization?Low-CodeUse Work Zone context bindings
Does your layout require multiple tabs, a wizard, or a custom chart library?Pro-CodeUse Component card
Do you need complex client-side validation or multi-step logic?Pro-CodeUse Component card
Will non-developers maintain or reconfigure the card post-deployment?Low-CodeDeclarative cards have a built-in admin UI
Are you wrapping an existing SAPUI5 app fragment?Pro-CodeComponent card is the right vessel

If the answer to most questions points to Low-Code but one layout requirement pushes toward Pro-Code, reconsider the layout requirement first. A different declarative type or a grouped Object card often solves what initially seems to need a custom component.

Project Structure and Tooling

A complete low-code card project in SAP Business Application Studio:

my-card-project/
├── manifest.json             ← Card definition (only required file)
├── i18n/
│   ├── i18n.properties       ← Default translations
│   └── i18n_de.properties    ← German translations
├── dt/
│   └── configuration.js      ← Design-time editor 
└── data/
    └── sample-data.json      ← Static data for BAS preview

Reference i18n keys anywhere in the manifest with double-brace syntax (same as parameters):

{
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.cards.orders",
    "type": "card",
    "i18n": "i18n/i18n.properties"
  },
  "sap.card": {
    "header": {
      "title": "{{CARD_TITLE}}",
      "subTitle": "{{CARD_SUBTITLE}}"
    }
  }
}
# i18n/i18n.properties
CARD_TITLE=Open Purchase Orders
CARD_SUBTITLE=Requires your attention

Summary

The key takeaways for architects designing content on SAP Build Work Zone for supplier portal scenarios:

  • Default to declarative. List, Table, Object, Analytical, and Timeline cards cover the standard supplier portal scenarios. The framework's rendering, theming, and Admin Console integration are worth preserving.
  • Use Work Zone context bindings ({context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}) to build personalized, identity-aware cards without server-side user resolution logic. This pattern is underused and more powerful than it looks.
  • Use binding expressions ({= ${field} > threshold ? 'Warning' : 'Success'}) for conditional UX — colours, icons, labels — without needing a controller.
  • Get the BTP destination right first. HTML5.DynamicDestination: true is not optional, and the July 2025 alias change in Standard Edition catches teams that haven't updated.
  • Reserve Component for genuine outliers — complex layouts or logic that the declarative model cannot express — and factor in the Admin Console governance cost before committing.

The full reference for all card types, manifest properties, and live examples is available in the SAP UI5 Card Explorer.

SAP UI5 Card Explorer

  • Card Explorer (all types, live examples)

entry.title: Principal Propagation from BTP to S/4HANA Public Cloud: Configuration Notes and Open Questions
entry.content:
Principal Propagation from BTP to S/4HANA Public Cloud: Configuration Notes and Open Questions

Upfront disclaimer: I have not yet run this end-to-end in a live landscape. What follows is the configuration path I've assembled from SAP Help, a handful of community posts, and my own reading of how the pieces connect. I'm posting it before testing because I couldn't find a single place that covers the Build Work Zone angle properly, and I'd rather have it corrected by people who've actually done it than sit on half-finished notes. Treat this as a starting point, not a verified runbook. If you spot something wrong, please say so in the comments, and I'll update the post.

The problem

We have BTP applications, mostly HTML5 apps surfaced through Build Work Zone, calling S/4HANA Public Cloud APIs. Today that goes through Communication Arrangements with a communication user, which works fine but means every request hits the backend as the same technical account. No per-user authorisation checks, no useful audit trail, and awkward conversations when someone asks who actually changed the purchase order.

So: principal propagation. And the first thing to internalise is that there is no Cloud Connector option here. Public Cloud has no X.509 principal propagation the way an on-premises system does. OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion is the path, and as far as I can tell, it's the only one.

How the flow actually works

It took me a while to get the mental model right, and I think this is where a lot of the confusion comes from:

  1. The user logs into Work Zone and gets a JWT from XSUAA (or via your IAS trust).
  2. The HTML5 app calls the backend through the managed approuter, which passes the user token to the Destination service.
  3. The Destination service builds a SAML assertion, puts the user's identity in the NameID, and signs it with the subaccount's Destination Trust certificate.
  4. It sends that to the S/4 OAuth token endpoint. The communication user's credentials authenticate the client here.
  5. S/4 validates the assertion, resolves the NameID to a business user, and returns a token carrying that user's authorisations.

The key point, and the thing I got wrong at first: the communication user is the OAuth client, not the identity being propagated. The business user is the subject. You need both, and they're unrelated objects.

Check this before you configure anything.

Open the Communication Scenario for the API you're targeting and confirm OAuth 2.0 appears as a supported inbound authentication method.

Many SAP-delivered A2X scenarios only offer Basic and X.509. If OAuth 2.0 isn't listed on the scenario, it won't be selectable on the Communication Arrangement either, and principal propagation is off the table for that API. From what I can gather, this is the single most common reason people report that it "doesn't work" when their config is actually fine.

If your scenario doesn't support it, your options are a Custom Communication Scenario built in ADT wrapping your own service, or finding a different standard scenario.

I'd genuinely like to know from anyone who's surveyed this: is there a list somewhere of which standard scenarios support OAuth 2.0 inbound? I've been checking them one at a time, and it's tedious.

S/4HANA Public Cloud configuration

Maintain Communication Users. Create one, save the password somewhere sensible. It becomes the client secret later.

Communication Systems. New system, then:

  • Host Name is your BTP subaccount subdomain
  • Tick OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider
  • Upload the certificate you exported from BTP Cockpit under Connectivity → Destinations → Destination Trust → Export (comes down as a .pem)
  • Copy the CN value from the uploaded certificate into the OAuth 2.0 SAML Issuer field.

That last step is easy to miss because the field does not populate itself. The certificate details render on screen, the CN sits right there, and nothing prompts you to copy it across.

There's a bigger trap sitting behind this one. You upload the Destination Trust certificate, not your XSUAA or IAS SAML metadata. My instinct was to register the identity provider, because that's the mental model everywhere else. But the assertion isn't signed by your IdP. The destination service signs it. If you've configured IAS as your subaccount trust and you upload the IAS metadata here, the assertion will be rejected, and the error message will not tell you why.

Communication Arrangements. Bind the scenario, the system and the user together, then set the inbound user's authentication method to OAuth 2.0. Once you save, the arrangement shows an OAuth 2.0 Details section containing the token endpoint, the SAML audience and the scope. Copy those exactly; don't reconstruct them by hand.

The BTP destination

Property Value

AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URLhttps://my<tenant>.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/opu/odata/sap/<SERVICE>
audienceS/4 tenant URL with no path, as shown in the arrangement
clientKeycommunication user name
tokenServiceURLhttps://my<tenant>-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
tokenServiceURLTypeDedicated
tokenServiceUsercommunication user name
tokenServicePasswordcommunication user password
nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress
userIdSourceemail
authnContextClassRefurn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
scopefrom the arrangement, e.g. API_BUSINESS_PARTNER_0001
compactAssertiontrue

Watch the token service host. It carries an -api suffix and is not the same host as the service URL.

One more thing on this table. Do not use the SystemUser property. SAP has deprecated it, and if it's set your propagation quietly collapses into a fixed technical user. Everything appears to work, the calls succeed, and the wrong name shows up in the backend. That's a nasty one to chase.

The Build Work Zone bits

This is the part I couldn't find written down anywhere in one piece.

Add HTML5.DynamicDestination: true to the destination. Without it the HTML5 app can't resolve the destination at runtime through the managed approuter.

Keep the destination in the same subaccount as the Work Zone site. Because the assertion is signed by that subaccount's Destination Trust certificate, and S/4 trusts exactly that certificate, a cross-subaccount setup breaks the chain.

Don't confuse this with HTML5.ForwardAuthToken. That property forwards the raw JWT and belongs to a different pattern (typically a CAP or Node backend). It has nothing to do with the SAML bearer exchange, and setting it here won't help.

And the user has to reach Work Zone through the identity provider whose email matches their S/4 business user. If your Work Zone SSO runs through IAS or Entra and the email on the S/4 business user is different, the assertion will be structurally valid, and the user lookup will still fail.

Identity mapping, which I suspect is where most of the pain lives

With userIdSource: email, S/4 looks up a business user by email address on an exact match. Which means:

  • The person needs an actual Business User in S/4, not just a communication user
  • Their email in S/4 has to match their email in BTP/IAS exactly
  • They need business roles covering the business catalogue behind the OData service

That third point deserves emphasis. Principal propagation enforces real authorisations, which is the entire reason you're doing it. A propagated user with no role gets a clean 403, and from the BTP side that looks identical to a broken propagation setup.

There's a commercial angle here too, and I'd flag it early with stakeholders rather than late. Every propagated user needs an S/4 business user and appropriate roles. If the plan was to let a few hundred Work Zone users read order data, the licensing conversation looks very different from the technical-user integration it's replacing. Worth raising before you build.

If you can't get email alignment, the alternative appears to be userIdSource: user_name with nameIdFormat: ...nameid-format:unspecified, mapping to the S/4 user ID instead. I haven't tried this variant.

Testing and error decoding

Check Connection in the cockpit only proves the endpoint is reachable. It does not exercise the SAML flow at all, which I found misleading. To actually test the exchange, you want to call the Destination service find API with a user token attached:

GET https://destination-configuration.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/<DEST_NAME>
Authorization: Bearer <client_token>
X-user-token: <user_jwt>

If authTokens[] comes back populated, the exchange worked. Then check the S/4 side to confirm which user actually arrived, because a successful exchange with the wrong subject is a real failure mode.

Errors I'd expect and what I think they mean:

Symptom Likely cause

invalid_grant, assertion rejectedSAML Issuer field empty or not matching the certificate CN, or wrong certificate uploaded
unauthorized_clientCommunication user credentials wrong, or the arrangement isn't set to OAuth 2.0
invalid_scopeScope doesn't match what the arrangement published
Token issues are fine, then 403 on the API callUser resolved correctly but has no business role for that catalogue
Token issues fine, wrong user in the backendSystemUser is set, or userIdSource is mismatched
Worked for months, then broke everywhere at onceDestination Trust certificate rotated and needs re-uploading to the Communication System.

That last row is one to put in the operations runbook now. The subaccount signing certificate has a finite validity, and nothing on the S/4 side warns you when it expires. I'd expect the failure to arrive as a total outage with no obvious trigger.

An alternative I'm still weighing

If you're fanning out to several backends, or the identity has to survive a hop through middleware, routing via Integration Suite with the SAML bearer flow on the outbound adapter would centralise the trust configuration in one place. It costs you a hop and a subscription, but it also means one place to fix when certificates rotate.

For a single Work Zone to S/4 path, I don't think it's justified. For a landscape with several BTP apps and multiple ERP tenants, I suspect it is. Interested in whether anyone has made that call in either direction and regretted it.

Sources

  • Principal Propagation from SAP Build Process Automation workflow to S/4HANA Public Cloud, which is recent and screenshot-level on the S/4 configuration
  • OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Flow with the SAP BTP Destination Service, S/4HANA Cloud, older, but it has the full destination JSON and the clearest explanation of Provider Name versus assertionIssuer
  • SAP Help: Scenario: User Propagation from the Cloud Foundry Environment to SAP S/4HANA Cloud, and the Set Up Authentication for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Extensions PDF

Over to you

I'll update this post once we've run it in our own landscape. In the meantime, if you've implemented this:

  • Did the Destination Trust certificate catch you out, or is that just me reading it wrong?
  • Is there a reliable way to see which standard communication scenarios support OAuth 2.0 inbound without opening each one?
  • How are you handling the business user and licensing side at scale?

entry.title: How I Enabled Support of bot Standalone and Managed Approuters in One SAPUI5 and SAP CAP Application
entry.content:
Supporting Standalone and Managed Approuters in One SAPUI5 and SAP CAP Application

Introduction

While developing an SAPUI5 application on SAP BTP, I encountered a requirement that initially appeared straightforward:

  • The application should be directly accessible through a standalone approuter.
  • The same application should also be available through SAP Build Work Zone using its managed approuter.
  • Both entry points should use the same SAPUI5 codebase and SAP CAP backend.
  • Authentication, authorization, and OData communication should work consistently in both environments.

The application worked correctly when accessed through the standalone approuter. However, when I opened the same application from SAP Build Work Zone, I started encountering HTTP 404 errors, authentication failures, incorrect OData paths, and Content Security Policy issues with SAPUI5 VizFrame charts.

I initially assumed that because both runtime models use an xs-app.json file, the same routing configuration and absolute OData URLs would work in both environments. I eventually discovered that this assumption was incorrect.

The standalone and managed approuters serve the application from different URL contexts. This seemingly small difference directly affects how frontend service URLs are resolved.

In this article, I explain the architecture I designed and developed to support both approuter models using:

  • A single SAPUI5 codebase
  • A single SAP CAP service
  • XSUAA-based authentication
  • User-token propagation
  • SAP Destination service
  • HTML5 Application Repository
  • SAP Build Work Zone
  • Separate routing configurations
  • Runtime-aware OData URL resolution

This article is based on a real implementation and includes the design decisions, dead ends, configuration, code, and troubleshooting lessons from that experience.

The problem I was trying to solve

The application needed to support two access patterns.

Direct application access

Users should be able to open the application through a dedicated Cloud Foundry route exposed by a standalone approuter.

The request flow should be:

Browser
   |
   v
Standalone Approuter
   |
   +---- Serves the SAPUI5 application
   |
   +---- Forwards OData requests
   |
   v
SAP CAP Service

SAP Build Work Zone access

The same application should be available as an SAP Fiori application inside SAP Build Work Zone.

The request flow should be:

Browser
   |
   v
SAP Build Work Zone
   |
   v
Managed Approuter
   |
   +---- Loads the application from the HTML5 Application Repository
   |
   +---- Resolves the backend destination
   |
   v
SAP CAP Service

I wanted to avoid maintaining separate SAPUI5 applications or separate frontend builds for these two environments.

The first issue I encountered

My application initially used root-relative OData paths:

const SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/my-service/";

This worked correctly through the standalone approuter because the application and the OData route were available from the same host root.

For example:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/odata/v4/my-service/

However, the managed approuter uses an application-specific prefix when serving an application from the HTML5 Application Repository.

A simplified managed-approuter URL can look like this:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/index.html

The corresponding OData request may need to retain that prefix:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

When I used a leading slash:

/odata/v4/my-service/

the browser resolved the request from the host root and discarded the application prefix.

The request therefore became:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/odata/v4/my-service/

instead of:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

This resulted in an HTTP 404 response.

The most surprising part of the investigation was that a single leading slash determined whether the application worked or failed. Because the same URL worked through the standalone approuter, I initially investigated destination configuration and XSUAA authorization instead of URL resolution.

The design decision

I considered using environment-specific service URLs:

if (managedApprouter) {
    // Use managed-approuter URL
} else {
    // Use standalone-approuter URL
}

Another option was to maintain separate frontend builds for each runtime.

I decided against both approaches because they would:

  • Duplicate configuration
  • Introduce environment-specific code
  • Make deployments harder to maintain
  • Increase the risk of one version behaving differently from the other
  • Require changes whenever an application name or route changed

Instead, I designed a URL resolver that derives the service URL from the SAPUI5 component’s actual runtime location.

This allows the application to preserve the managed-approuter prefix while still supporting local CAP execution and the standalone approuter.

Project structure

The relevant project structure is:

project-root/
|
|-- app/
|   |
|   |-- my-ui5-app/
|       |
|       |-- webapp/
|       |   |-- controller/
|       |   |-- model/
|       |   |   |-- serviceUrl.js
|       |   |-- Component.js
|       |   |-- manifest.json
|       |   |-- index.html
|       |
|       |-- xs-app.json
|
|-- router/
|   |-- package.json
|   |-- xs-app.json
|
|-- srv/
|   |-- service.cds
|   |-- service.js
|
|-- xs-security.json
|-- mta.yaml
|-- package.json

Two xs-app.json files are intentionally maintained:

  • router/xs-app.json configures the standalone approuter.
  • app/my-ui5-app/xs-app.json configures the managed-approuter runtime.

Although the files have similar backend routes, they serve frontend content differently.

Standalone approuter implementation

Standalone approuter package

The standalone approuter is a Node.js Cloud Foundry application using @SAP/approuter.

The router/package.json can be defined as follows:

{
  "name": "my-standalone-approuter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "@sap/approuter": "^20.0.0"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js"
  }
}

The approuter itself does not contain application business logic. It handles responsibilities such as:

  • User authentication
  • Route matching
  • Forwarding requests
  • Token propagation
  • Serving frontend resources

Standalone xs-app.json

The standalone approuter serves the SAPUI5 application from its local webapp directory and forwards OData requests to the SAP CAP service.

{
  "welcomeFile": "index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/api-docs(.*)$",
      "target": "/api-docs$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "localDir": "webapp",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
    }
  ]
}

OData route

The following route captures requests beginning with /odata/:

{
  "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
  "target": "/odata/$1",
  "destination": "srv-api",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "csrfProtection": false
}

For example:

/odata/v4/my-service/Requests

is forwarded to:

<srv-api>/odata/v4/my-service/Requests

Frontend route

The final route serves the SAPUI5 files:

{
  "source": "^/(.*)$",
  "localDir": "webapp",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
}

This works because the standalone approuter module contains a copy of the built SAPUI5 webapp content.

Managed approuter implementation

In the managed-approuter scenario, I did not serve the frontend from the standalone router’s local directory.

Instead:

  1. The SAPUI5 application is built.
  2. The application is packaged as a ZIP archive.
  3. The archive is uploaded to the HTML5 Application Repository.
  4. SAP Build Work Zone discovers the application.
  5. The managed approuter loads it from the repository.
  6. Backend requests are forwarded through a destination.

Managed xs-app.json

The managed-approuter configuration belongs to the HTML5 application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/api-docs(.*)$",
      "target": "/api-docs$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^(.*)$",
      "target": "$1",
      "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
    }
  ]
}

The important difference is the frontend route:

{
  "source": "^(.*)$",
  "target": "$1",
  "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa"
}

Instead of using:

"localDir": "webapp"

the managed approuter loads the application through:

"service": "html5-apps-repo-rt"

This distinction is fundamental.

Runtime Frontend source
Standalone approuterLocal application directory
Managed approuterHTML5 Application Repository runtime

Dynamic OData URL resolution

The key part of my design was to stop treating the OData endpoint as a fixed root-relative URL.

Instead of this:

const SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/my-service/";

I used a relative service path:

const SERVICE_URL = "odata/v4/my-service/";

I then introduced a reusable SAPUI5 URL-resolution module.

serviceUrl.js

sap.ui.define([], () => {
    "use strict";

    const LOCAL_CAP_APP_PATH = /\/my-ui5-app(?:\/webapp)?\/?$/;

    function resolve(sUri) {
        const sRelativeUri = String(sUri || "").replace(/^\/+/, "");

        const oComponentBaseUrl = new URL(
            sap.ui.require.toUrl("my/ui5/app/"),
            window.location.href
        );

        /*
         * During local CAP execution, the UI may be served below:
         *
         * /my-ui5-app/webapp
         *
         * while the CAP OData service is exposed from:
         *
         * /odata
         */
        if (LOCAL_CAP_APP_PATH.test(oComponentBaseUrl.pathname)) {
            return new URL(
                `/${sRelativeUri}`,
                oComponentBaseUrl.origin
            ).toString();
        }

        /*
         * For a managed approuter, retain the HTML5 application
         * prefix by resolving the path relative to the component.
         */
        return new URL(
            sRelativeUri,
            oComponentBaseUrl
        ).toString();
    }

    return {
        resolve
    };
});

Replace the following values with your application-specific values:

/my-ui5-app/

and:

"my/ui5/app/"

The namespace should correspond to the SAPUI5 application namespace.

Why this resolver works

Local CAP runtime

Suppose the application is served locally from:

http://localhost:4004/my-ui5-app/webapp/

The resolver recognizes the local CAP application path and produces:

http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/my-service/

Standalone approuter

Suppose the application is served from:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/

The service URL resolves to:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/odata/v4/my-service/

Managed approuter

Suppose the SAPUI5 component is served from:

https://<managed-host>/<application-prefix>/

The relative service path resolves to:

https://<managed-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

The managed-approuter application prefix remains intact.

Using the resolver in the SAPUI5 application

The service constants should not start with /:

const SERVICE_V2_URL = "odata/v2/my-service/";
const SERVICE_V4_URL = "odata/v4/my-service/";

The resolver can then be imported into a controller or component.

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/UIComponent",
    "my/ui5/app/model/serviceUrl"
], function (
    UIComponent,
    serviceUrl
) {
    "use strict";

    return UIComponent.extend("my.ui5.app.Component", {
        metadata: {
            manifest: "json"
        },

        init: function () {
            UIComponent.prototype.init.apply(this, arguments);

            const sServiceUrl = serviceUrl.resolve(
                "odata/v4/my-service/"
            );

            console.log("Resolved service URL:", sServiceUrl);

            this.getRouter().initialize();
        }
    });
});

It can also be used for direct fetch calls:

const sUrl = serviceUrl.resolve(
    "odata/v4/my-service/getDashboardData"
);

fetch(sUrl, {
    method: "GET",
    credentials: "include",
    headers: {
        "Accept": "application/json"
    }
})
    .then(function (oResponse) {
        if (!oResponse.ok) {
            throw new Error(
                `Request failed with status ${oResponse.status}`
            );
        }

        return oResponse.json();
    })
    .then(function (oData) {
        console.log(oData);
    });

XSUAA authentication configuration

The application uses XSUAA for user authentication and role-based authorization.

A simplified xs-security.json can look like this:

{
  "xsappname": "my-application",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "name": "$XSAPPNAME.User",
      "description": "Application user access"
    },
    {
      "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin",
      "description": "Application administrator access"
    }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    {
      "name": "User",
      "description": "Application user",
      "scope-references": [
        "$XSAPPNAME.User"
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "Admin",
      "description": "Application administrator",
      "scope-references": [
        "$XSAPPNAME.User",
        "$XSAPPNAME.Admin"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

After deployment:

  1. Create the required role collections.
  2. Add the generated role templates.
  3. Assign the role collections to the relevant users or identity-provider groups.

A successful login only confirms that the identity provider authenticated the user. It does not automatically mean that the user has every application scope.

MTA configuration

The MTA contains the following major components:

SAP CAP service
Standalone approuter
SAPUI5 HTML5 module
HTML5 application content deployer
Destination content module
XSUAA service
Destination service
HTML5 repository host
HTML5 repository runtime

The following excerpts show the important relationships.

SAP CAP service module

modules:
  - name: my-application-srv
    type: nodejs
    path: gen/srv

    provides:
      - name: srv-api
        properties:
          srv-url: ${default-url}

    requires:
      - name: my-application-auth

    parameters:
      buildpack: nodejs_buildpack
      memory: 512M

The service exposes its runtime URL through the srv-api dependency:

provides:
  - name: srv-api
    properties:
      srv-url: ${default-url}

Standalone approuter module

  - name: my-application-router
    type: approuter.nodejs
    path: gen/router

    requires:
      - name: srv-api
        group: destinations
        properties:
          name: srv-api
          url: ~{srv-url}
          forwardAuthToken: true

      - name: my-application-auth

      - name: my-application-destination

      - name: my-application-html5-runtime

The following configuration propagates the logged-in user’s token to the CAP service:

forwardAuthToken: true

Without token forwarding, the CAP service may receive an anonymous or technically incomplete request and return HTTP 401 or 403.

SAPUI5 HTML5 module

  - name: my-ui5-app
    type: html5
    path: app/my-ui5-app

    build-parameters:
      builder: custom
      commands:
        - npm ci
        - npm run build
      supported-platforms: []
      build-result: dist

HTML5 application deployer

  - name: my-application-app-content
    type: com.sap.application.content
    path: .

    requires:
      - name: my-application-html5-host
        parameters:
          content-target: true

    build-parameters:
      build-result: resources
      requires:
        - name: my-ui5-app
          artifacts:
            - my-ui5-app.zip
          target-path: resources/

This module uploads the built SAPUI5 application to the HTML5 Application Repository.

Destination content module

  - name: my-application-destination-content
    type: com.sap.application.content

    requires:
      - name: my-application-destination
        parameters:
          content-target: true

      - name: my-application-html5-host
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: my-application-html5-host-key

      - name: my-application-auth
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: my-application-auth-key

      - name: srv-api

    parameters:
      content:
        instance:
          destinations:
            - Name: srv-api
              Type: HTTP
              ProxyType: Internet
              URL: ~{srv-api/srv-url}
              Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange
              HTML5.DynamicDestination: true
              HTML5.ForwardAuthToken: true

          existing_destinations_policy: update

For the managed-approuter flow, I used:

Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange

This allows the destination to exchange and propagate the logged-in user’s security context when calling the protected CAP service.

Required resources

resources:
  - name: my-application-auth
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: xsuaa
      service-plan: application
      path: ./xs-security.json

  - name: my-application-destination
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: destination
      service-plan: lite
      config:
        HTML5Runtime_enabled: true

  - name: my-application-html5-host
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-host

  - name: my-application-html5-runtime
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-runtime

Connecting the application to SAP Build Work Zone

The SAPUI5 manifest.json should contain the appropriate sap.cloud configuration:

{
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "my.ui5.app",
    "type": "application",
    "applicationVersion": {
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
  },
  "sap.cloud": {
    "public": true,
    "service": "my.application.service"
  }
}

The same sap.cloud.service value must be used consistently in the destination content where applicable.

For example:

sap.cloud.service: my.application.service

I found that a mismatch here could make the deployment succeed while preventing the application from being discovered or resolved correctly in the Work Zone content provider.

After deployment:

  1. Open SAP Build Work Zone administration.
  2. Open the Channel Manager or content provider configuration.
  3. Refresh the HTML5 Apps content provider.
  4. Add the application to My Content.
  5. Assign it to a role.
  6. Add it to a workspace, page, or site.
  7. Ensure the user has the corresponding Work Zone role assignment and XSUAA role collection.

Content Security Policy and VizFrame

After solving the OData routing problem, I encountered another issue: the reports page worked in SAP Build Work Zone, but the charts failed through the standalone approuter.

The browser console displayed an error similar to:

Creating a worker from 'blob:...' violates the following
Content Security Policy directive: "script-src ..."

It also displayed:

Failed to construct 'Worker'

I initially investigated the VizFrame chart configuration because the chart controls were not rendering. However, the chart data and bindings were correct.

The actual problem was that the visualization library attempted to create a web worker using a blob: URL, but the application’s Content Security Policy did not allow it.

I updated the CSP in index.html:

<meta
    http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
    content="
        default-src 'self';
        script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        worker-src 'self' blob:;
        style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        font-src 'self' data:
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        img-src 'self' data: blob:
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        connect-src 'self'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
    "
/>

The important addition was:

worker-src 'self' blob:;

The final CSP should be reviewed according to the organization’s security requirements. Permissions such as 'unsafe-eval' should not be added automatically unless required by the selected SAPUI5 version or application behavior and accepted by the relevant security team.

CSRF protection

The routing examples in this article show:

"csrfProtection": false

This reflects the implementation being discussed, but it should not be interpreted as a recommendation to disable CSRF protection for every route.

For state-changing OData requests, such as:

  • POST
  • PATCH
  • PUT
  • DELETE

the safer approach is to use the OData model’s built-in CSRF handling or explicitly fetch and send a CSRF token.

For example:

X-CSRF-Token: Fetch

The selected approach should be aligned with:

  • The CAP service behavior
  • The SAPUI5 OData model
  • The application’s authentication model
  • Organizational security standards
  • Whether the endpoint is read-only or state-changing

Building and deploying the application

Install the project dependencies:

npm install

Build the CAP project:

npx cds build --production

Build the MTA archive:

mbt build

Log in to the target Cloud Foundry environment:

cf login -a https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Select the correct organization and space:

cf target -o "<organization>" -s "<space>"

Deploy the MTA archive:

cf deploy mta_archives/<archive-name>.mtar

After deployment, verify the application through both entry points.

Standalone approuter

https://<standalone-approuter-route>/

Managed approuter

Open the application through SAP Build Work Zone or the relevant HTML5 application runtime entry point.

Troubleshooting lessons from my implementation

HTTP 404 for OData requests only in SAP Build Work Zone

Symptom

The UI loads, but the OData request returns HTTP 404.

What I initially assumed

I initially treated this as a missing destination or incorrect backend route.

Actual cause

The OData request used a root-relative URL:

/odata/v4/my-service/

This removed the managed-approuter application prefix.

Resolution

Use a component-relative path:

odata/v4/my-service/

and resolve it against the SAPUI5 component location.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized

Possible causes

  • Missing or invalid XSUAA binding
  • Expired authentication session
  • Missing token propagation
  • Destination using the wrong authentication method
  • Direct access to the CAP service instead of access through the approuter

Important lesson

An HTTP 401 response does not always mean the role configuration is wrong. I learned to inspect the complete request URL first.

If the request reached the wrong route because its application prefix was missing, changing scopes or role collections would not solve the problem.

HTTP 403 Forbidden

Possible causes

  • The user is authenticated but lacks the required scope
  • The correct role collection was not assigned
  • The destination propagated a technical token instead of the user token
  • The CAP authorization annotation rejected the user
  • Application-level user provisioning rejected the user

Difference between 401 and 403

A simplified interpretation is:

401: The request does not have acceptable authentication.
403: The identity is known, but it does not have permission.

Application works through Work Zone but not through the standalone approuter

Check the following:

  • Does the standalone approuter contain the built webapp content?
  • Does router/xs-app.json use localDir?
  • Is the standalone approuter bound to XSUAA?
  • Is the srv-api destination injected?
  • Is forwardAuthToken enabled?
  • Is the frontend route placed after the more specific OData routes?

Route order matters because the generic frontend route can otherwise capture requests intended for the backend.

Application works through the standalone approuter but not through Work Zone

Check the following:

  • Was the SAPUI5 ZIP uploaded to the HTML5 Application Repository?
  • Does the HTML5 application contain its own xs-app.json?
  • Is HTML5Runtime_enabled set correctly?
  • Does the destination exist?
  • Does the destination name exactly match srv-api?
  • Is sap.cloud.service consistent?
  • Was the Work Zone content provider refreshed?
  • Was the application assigned to the required role and site?
  • Does the OData URL preserve the managed-approuter application prefix?

Charts fail only in one runtime

Open the browser console and look for:

Content Security Policy

or:

Failed to construct Worker

If VizFrame uses a blob worker, verify that the CSP contains:

worker-src 'self' blob:;

This was particularly instructive because the problem appeared to be in the chart implementation, while the actual cause was browser security policy.

Missing i18n files

SAPUI5 may attempt to load locale-specific files such as:

i18n/i18n_en.properties
i18n/i18n_en_GB.properties

If these files are not available, the browser can display HTTP 404 warnings.

Depending on the application’s localization strategy, either create the required files or verify that the fallback bundle is configured correctly.

Architecture summary

The final architecture I implemented can be summarized as follows:

                           +-------------------------+
                           |       SAP CAP Service   |
                           |     Protected by XSUAA  |
                           +------------+------------+
                                        ^
                                        |
                              User token forwarding
                                        |
                  +---------------------+---------------------+
                  |                                           |
       +----------+-----------+                   +-----------+-----------+
       | Standalone Approuter |                   |   Managed Approuter   |
       | Cloud Foundry App    |                   | SAP Build Work Zone   |
       +----------+-----------+                   +-----------+-----------+
                  |                                           |
       Local SAPUI5 content                       HTML5 App Repository
                  |                                           |
                  +---------------------+---------------------+
                                        |
                              Same SAPUI5 codebase

The two runtimes have different routing responsibilities, but they use the same application logic.

What I would do differently next time

Looking back, I would validate the application through both approuter models much earlier in the development cycle.

My initial local and standalone-approuter testing gave me confidence that the routing was complete. However, it did not expose the managed-approuter prefix behavior.

For a future implementation, I would test these scenarios from the beginning:

  1. Local CAP runtime
  2. Standalone approuter
  3. Managed approuter
  4. Direct OData read
  5. State-changing OData request
  6. Role-restricted request
  7. VizFrame or worker-based UI functionality
  8. Session expiry and reauthentication

I would also inspect the final browser request URL before changing destination or authorization configurations. That simple step would have shortened my troubleshooting considerably.

Key takeaways

The most important lesson from this implementation is that supporting both approuter models is not simply a matter of deploying two routers.

The frontend URL strategy, destination configuration, authentication flow, HTML5 application packaging, and runtime routing must all work together.

My main takeaways were:

  • Do not assume identical-looking URLs behave identically across runtime models.
  • Avoid root-relative service URLs when an application may run behind a managed-approuter prefix.
  • Resolve backend URLs relative to the SAPUI5 component.
  • Keep runtime-specific routing configurations separate.
  • Keep the frontend business logic shared.
  • Forward the authenticated user token to protected CAP services.
  • Do not assume every HTTP 401 or 404 response is caused by XSUAA.
  • Verify the complete browser request URL before changing authorization settings.
  • Ensure sap.cloud.service values are consistent.
  • Treat Content Security Policy as part of the application architecture.
  • Test both runtime models early rather than after the application is complete.

The design allowed me to support direct access and SAP Build Work Zone access using one SAPUI5 codebase and one SAP CAP backend, without hard-coded deployment URLs or duplicated frontend applications.

I hope this experience helps other SAP BTP architects and developers who encounter the same routing and authentication challenges.

I would be interested to hear how others have designed applications that need to support both standalone and managed approuters.

entry.title: BTP Success Plans from SAP in Action with real Experiences from the Field
entry.content:
We recently ran a webinar on how the Advanced and Max Success Plans work for SAP Business AI Platform (BAIP) and SAP Business Technology (BTP) customers. Together with Amit Lodhe, Global Service Solution Advisory Leader for SAP Business AI Platform, and Dilek Cevikalp, Customer Success Manager for BTP and BAIP, we walked through what these service plans deliver, showed real customer engagements and discussed open questions.  

This post summarizes the key points for anyone who is currently evaluating Success Plans for BTP/ BAIP, thinking about AI adoption on BTP in general, or wondering how the new Success Plan approach compares to what they had before.

The challenges SAP BTP customers face today

Let me start with what we hear regularly from BTP customers. Three themes keep coming up:

  • Slow innovation speed and limited AI adoption. Customers have BTP in place, they see the potential of Business AI, but they struggle to move from "we should do something with AI" to an actual implementation path. And the technology landscape is evolving fast.
  • Increased risk from excessive customization. Many organizations carry a lot of custom logic. When they want to modernize or adopt new capabilities, the complexity of their landscape creates risk. They need expert guidance to make the right architectural decisions, not just documentation.
  • Lack of holistic integration across platforms and applications. BTP connects multiple SAP and non-SAP systems. Getting identity management, connectivity, security, and process orchestration right requires more than self-service content. It requires hands-on expertise at the right moment.

The Advanced and Max Success Plans are designed to address these (and other) challenges. They provide structured guidance, dedicated expertise, and a collaborative engagement model that goes well beyond reactive support.

What the Advanced and Max Success Plans cover for BTP and BAIP

The core idea is that you get a Customer Success Manager (CSM) who orchestrates a tailored Advanced Success plan for you. The CSM acts as your single point of coordination. They build your adoption plan, position the right services, order them, and orchestrate their delivery across quarters. For Max Success Plan this orchestrating role is called "Success Plan Manager", who also can support onsite.

On the expert side, so called Success Experts provide deep subject matter expertise to help you adopt, optimize, and get full value from your SAP cloud solutions. This is not a help desk. It is a structured engagement with regular service planning, adoption checkpoints, and innovation checkpoints throughout the year.

CSM and Success Expert collaboration model with regular checkpoints.

You might ask yourself how the different Success Plan tiers work in practice:

The Advanced Success Plan includes orchestration of the success plan with Success Expert sessions, innovation and adoption guidance, activation and optimization sessions, AI-driven quality and process guidance, and enhanced support SLAs (50% faster initial response on priority 2, 3, and 4 incidents). Compared to the former Preferred Success offering, the Advanced plan delivers more value at the same price point as the former Standard Preferred Success. Customers now get also activation and optimization sessions and Success Expert engagement included, which previously required the more expensive Expanded Edition.

The Max Success Plan adds everything from Advanced plus cross-solution process improvement services, transformation advisory services, tailored AI use case adoption services, the dedicated Success Plan Manager (an evolution of the TQM role), premium support response SLAs, and support case management assistance. 

The Max Success plan is designed for complex landscapes where customers need large-scale, on-site, workshop-type engagements that deliver highly customized results. These premium services are consumed against so called premium service days.

One key differentiator across both tiers is, that the services from the Advanced layer are unlimited. There is no cap on how many services can be delivered per year, as long as they are part of your service plan. To put that into perspective, Amit shared the example of a Japanese customer who consumed more than 120 services in 18 months.

Customer Example 1: From "Where do we start with AI?" to a concrete pilot

The first case study involves a utilities IT services provider. They are an internal shared services organization supporting multiple utilities businesses. They already had RISE with SAP and were actively using BTP. The foundation was in place so to say.

When their internal business units started requesting AI capabilities, the IT team was unsure and hit a wall. They had identified a compelling use case: automating business partner creation from incoming emails. But they had no AI expertise internally and no clear implementation path. Multiple AI use cases from different lines of business were piling up, with no way to evaluate or prioritize them.

Three Advanced Success Plan services were activated:

  • AI Readiness Workshop for SAP Business AI - a full-day session with the complete technical team of eight participants
  • AI Workshop - dedicated follow-up to deepen the practical understanding
  • Expert AI Guidance for BTP Implementation -after connecting the customer's team with an SAP AI expert

The structured engagement replaced uncertainty with clear steps. The AI Core architecture was explained, the pilot use case was defined, and the IT team came out of the workshops equipped to build AI use cases independently. The pilot scope was agreed, and the next phase involves expert engagement directly on the customer's own landscape, moving from learning to building.

This engagement is still in progress. Dilek the CSM continues to orchestrate follow-up services as the customer's AI journey evolves.

Customer Example 2: From architectural uncertainty to a go-live with 4,200 employees

The second case is a large grid operator with approximately 4,200 employees. Their goal was to roll out Work Zone Advanced as their central employee portal.

The challenges were different here but equally blocking. The architectural decision between Work Zone Standard and Work Zone Advanced was unresolved. Identity management was in conflict because Microsoft's and SAP's recommendations contradicted. And the manual effort in content provisioning put scalability at risk.

The Advanced Success Plan services here were the following:

  • Architecture Review for SAP Work Zone: expert validation of the right BTP approach
  • Expert Guidance: a full-day BTP workshop covering Work Zone architecture, Integration Suite, and AI services
  • Strategic Assessment: coordination to resolve the identity management conflict

All of this was orchestrated through Dilek the CSM. Multiple SAP specialists were brought in, each for their specific domain, but the customer had a single point of coordination throughout.

The result was the achieved go-live. All 4,200 employees are now live on Work Zone Advanced. The Standard vs. Advanced decision was made with confidence, without rework or guesswork. Identity management is resolved with clean authentication and security. The foundation is stable and scalable, with manual effort significantly reduced.

What is particularly interesting about this case is what happened next. The customer is now evaluating AI use cases including fraud detection and a payment verification agent. The CSM is already developing the next iteration of the success plan to cover these new priorities. That iterative nature of the engagement is central to how the model works.

The Success Plan service portfolio consists of more than 100 services

Behind the individual customer stories sits a comprehensive service portfolio. Amit walked us through what he called the "super catalogue". This are more than 100 services across all BTP modules.

The portfolio is structured around four promised outcomes:

  1. Continuous long-term engagement with increased productivity. The product expert helps you gain productivity in your execution, as both customer cases demonstrated.
  2. Reimagined processes and accelerated innovation. Through product guidance and innovation adoption guidance, manual and semi-automated processes are replaced.
  3. Adoption of next-generation capabilities and optimized processes with reduced TCO. Activation and optimization sessions involve hands-on configuration work done by SAP directly in your landscape. Trust management, IPS, IAS configuration, connectivity activation, Joule agent activation, AI Core activation — these are configurations that keep the ground ready. A recommendation is to separate core implementation activities (which you can leave for your partner) from non-core activation activities (divert those to the success plan).
  4. Improved operations, performance, and business continuity. Enhanced SLAs provide 50% faster response times during critical phases like go-live.

Portfolio elements across BAIP Technology Foundation (BTP) modules

The services cover platform foundations (BTP administration, security, connectivity), SAP Integration Suite (from foundation to PI/PO migration to custom integrations and governance), application development (SAP Build, ABAP Cloud, Clean Core, DevOps), artificial intelligence (AI Core, Joule, Joule Studio, AI data layer, AI strategy), and automation (process automation, cognitive automation).

For customers with a specific focus on AI, there is a dedicated recommended service plan that covers AI data layer strategy, AI business scenario design, Joule foundations, Joule Studio, and AI Core enablement. And for organizations looking at the broader agentic AI journey, a cross-line-of-business service plan addresses everything from AI orientation and use case navigation to AI trust and compliance, change management, and AI CoE foundation.

Fast Path to Agentic AI

The change management point deserves also some emphasis. When you start introducing AI agents to your workforce and AI agents become an integral part of people's work profiles, that is a significant organizational change. The success plan portfolio includes dedicated organizational change management services delivered by SAP consulting experts. This is not technical change management. It covers the people, process, and governance dimensions that determine whether AI adoption actually sticks.

Customers on the Max Success Plan benefit from services across the full BTP solution lifecycle from Discover through Run covering platform foundation, enterprise integration, application extension, process automation, and artificial intelligence. These services, such as architecture transformation, transformation safeguarding, and business transformation management, are minimum 10 to 15 days in scope and designed for complex, large-scale engagements. Services in this plan are grouped by business scenarios like "Modernize Your Integration Landscape with SAP Integration Suite", "Accelerate Your Business Transformation with a Clean Core", or "Empower Your Business with AI with SAP BTP", which helps customers identify the right entry point.

What does this new Success Plan approach mean for BTP customers?

If you are a BTP customer today, the practical implication is, that you do not need to figure out AI adoption, integration architecture, or platform optimization on your own or in pieces. The success plan model provides structured, expert-led engagement that evolves with your priorities.

The customer examples show the range. One started from zero AI knowledge and ended with a scoped pilot and an enabled team. The other resolved complex architectural decisions and achieved a go-live for 4,200 employees. Both cases share a common thread: a single CSM orchestrating the right experts at the right time, with a service plan that adapts as new questions and priorities emerge. (See the slides below for additional examples). For customers coming from Preferred Success, the transition to the Advanced Success Plan brings more value at the same price point. For organizations with complex landscapes and strategic transformation needs, the Max Success Plan adds the premium services that make a measurable difference.

Next steps

If you want to explore how a Success Plan fits your BTP or AI priorities:

  • Talk to your SAP account team. They can recommend whether the Advanced or Max Success Plan is the right fit, based on your landscape and engagement history.
  • If you already have an engagement (for example, a Preferred Success plan or Premium Engagement contracts), ask about transitioning to the Advanced or Max Success Plan.
  • Reach out to us directly if you are not sure who your SAP contact is - we are happy to help you find the right people.

Questions and Answers from the BAIP Success Plan webinar

Several questions came up during the session. Here are the most relevant ones:

How does the Advanced Success Plan compare to the former Preferred Success? The former Preferred Success had two editions: Standard and Expanded. The Expanded Edition included activation and optimization services and Success Expert engagement, but at a higher price. The Advanced Success Plan now offers those features at the same price as the former Standard Preferred Success. In other words: more value, same investment.

Are there limits on how many services can be consumed? No. As long as services are part of your service plan (created by the CSM and Success Expert), there is no cap. The Japanese customer example with 120+ services in 18 months illustrates the scale that is possible.

Are the activation services different between Advanced and Max? The activation and optimization services are identical. They come primarily from the Advanced tier. Max customers get everything from Advanced plus better SLA and the premium transformation services (cross-solution process improvement, transformation advisory, tailored AI use case adoption). Those premium services are consumed against dedicated premium days.

Can Success Plans be sold through partners? Yes. Success Plans can be sold via the partner channel. In indirect engagements, part of the CSM function is taken over by the partner, who upskills their resources to fulfil that role. There is a clear delineation of responsibilities between SAP and partner, which the account team can provide.

What is covered from the BTP portfolio? Almost all cloudified parts of the BAIP Technology Foundation are covered. This includes Integration Suite, SAP Build, AI Core, Platform Foundation, and related technologies. Third-party products integrated into the BAIP portfolio are not covered.
